entities.summary:
Quintus Tineius Clemens was a Roman senator who played a crucial role in shaping the political landscape of the 2nd century AD. As Consul Ordinarius in AD 195, he worked closely with Publius Julius Scapula Tertullus Priscus to address the growing tensions between the Roman Senate and the Emperor. Their efforts helped to maintain stability in the empire, but also underscored the growing power of the imperial administration.

Clemens' significance extends beyond his specific role, as he represents a key moment in the evolution of the Roman Senate and its relationship with the Emperor. His legacy can be seen in the continued struggle for power and influence between these two institutions, which would shape the course of Roman history for centuries to come.

The impact of Clemens' actions can be seen in the subsequent careers of his colleagues and successors, including the Emperor Commodus, who would go on to rule the empire for nearly two decades.

In the end, Clemens' story serves as a reminder of the complex web of alliances and rivalries that characterized the Roman imperial system, and the ways in which individual actions can have far-reaching consequences for the course of history.
